name: message-endpoint
intent: Connect an application to a messaging channel through a named, isolated component that turns application data into messages and back again, so the rest of the application stays unaware of message formats, channels and the messaging client API.
problem: An application must send or receive messages over a messaging channel, but its domain code must not be littered with connection, session, serialization and acknowledgement calls: without a dedicated place for the send/receive code, messaging API details and their failure modes spread through the codebase, and every additional channel, queue or broker client multiplies the duplication.
context: Enterprise integration and distributed systems where applications exchange messages through a messaging system (queues, topics, brokers, event streams) instead of calling each other directly. It applies at the seam between an application and the messaging infrastructure, on both the sending and the receiving side, and it is the entry point for the further endpoint decisions - event-driven vs. polling consumption, selective consumption, durable subscriptions, transactional clients - that only matter once such a component exists.
benefits: Domain code depends on ordinary methods and application types; channel names, headers, serialization and delivery tags stay inside one component.

One place to change when the transport, broker client or wire format changes: the endpoint is the only code that touches the messaging system, instead of publish/consume calls scattered across the codebase.
The application stays testable without a broker: the endpoint can be replaced by an in-process double or a fake implementation of the send/receive interface.
Operational concerns get a designated owner: acknowledgements, redelivery, idempotency, reconnect and error routing are localised in the endpoint instead of being implicit in every handler.

It is the substrate for the other endpoint patterns: the same component can grow into a Messaging Gateway, Service Activator, Durable Subscriber or Selective Consumer without touching application code.
tradeoffs: It is per-application glue: unless the sending side is generalised into a Messaging Gateway, every application writes its own endpoint and the same translation logic is duplicated across services.
The extra layer invites a God endpoint that accumulates transport policy, message format and business logic in one class - precisely the coupling the pattern is meant to prevent.

Acknowledgement, idempotency and reconnection become application responsibilities: a subtle endpoint bug (ack before processing, lost reconnect, swallowed error) turns into message loss or duplicate processing that the broker cannot repair.
It does not by itself decouple message formats: without a Messaging Mapper the wire schema still leaks into the endpoint's translation code and from there into the application.
Every endpoint needs its own tests and monitoring, and without a broker double those tests degenerate into slow integration tests.

participants.responsibility: The named, isolated component at the application boundary: it builds and parses messages, translates between application objects and the wire representation, and owns the interaction with the messaging client.
Domain code on either side; it hands data to the endpoint or receives application objects from it and assumes no knowledge of channels, message headers or the messaging API.
The messaging system's client API - connection, session or channel, producer and consumer objects - which the endpoint encapsulates and keeps out of the application.
The queue or topic the endpoint sends to or consumes from; it is selected by configuration rather than hard-coded in domain logic.
The envelope the endpoint builds or parses: payload plus metadata such as headers, correlation identifiers, content type and delivery annotations.
The runtime that invokes the endpoint when a message arrives (event-driven consumer) or when the application polls (polling consumer); it owns concurrency, prefetch and transaction boundaries.

use_cases: A service that publishes domain events to a topic and subscribes to the commands it must handle, keeping its domain layer free of broker client types.
A legacy application that must be integrated with several other applications over a message broker; the endpoint is the seam on which the adapter and gateway arrangements are then built.
A worker process whose only job is consuming tasks from a queue, executing them and acknowledging the outcome with explicit retry and dead-letter behaviour.

Replacing a synchronous remote call between two services with asynchronous messaging: the caller keeps its method call and the callee keeps its service method, while endpoints on both sides absorb the messaging.
A polyglot ecosystem where each application is written in a different language but all must speak the same messaging infrastructure; each language's endpoint realisation hides its own client library.
A Spring AMQP service exposes @RabbitListener methods backed by listener containers and uses RabbitTemplate for outbound messages, keeping RabbitMQ client details at the endpoint.
A Java worker wraps the AWS SDK for Java SqsClient sendMessage, receiveMessage and deleteMessage operations in producer and consumer endpoints, deleting only after processing succeeds.
A Kafka service puts Apache Kafka Producer and Consumer APIs behind separate topic endpoints, keeping serializers, consumer offsets and broker-specific records out of domain code.
avoid_when: Both sides live in one process: a thread-safe queue, an actor mailbox or plain in-process events is simpler and does not burden the code with serialization or broker failure semantics it does not need.

The application already runs on a framework that owns the messaging integration end to end (message-driven bean containers, Spring or NestJS listeners, Akka/Pekko stream connectors): configure the framework's endpoint instead of writing a second abstraction on top of it.
The integration is a single request/response call to one service: an HTTP/RPC client or the framework's gateway class is simpler and comes with the error semantics and tooling you actually need.

The code is a one-shot script whose message handling is genuinely trivial and will not grow: an inline publish/consume call is defensible; introduce the endpoint when the second caller or the second channel appears.
anti_patterns: Business logic inside the endpoint: message parsing, transport calls and domain rules fused into one class, so neither can be tested or reused independently.
Leaking the messaging API: handlers that receive broker-specific message or envelope types, and domain objects that know about channels, sessions and delivery tags.
One God endpoint consuming every channel and dispatching internally through a growing switch; route in the broker (routers, datatype channels) or split the endpoints instead.
Fire-and-forget publishing for business-critical commands with no confirms, correlation identifier or dead-letter path, so failures disappear silently.
Acknowledging before processing (auto-ack), which silently converts at-least-once delivery into message loss on crash.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: messaging mechanics, message format and domain behaviour are three different responsibilities, and the endpoint owns only the first two.

Dependency inversion / ports and adapters: the application depends on an application-shaped interface and the endpoint adapts the messaging client to it - the messaging-specific case of a hexagonal boundary.
Information hiding: channel names, headers, delivery tags and client types are implementation details of the endpoint.
Single responsibility per endpoint: one endpoint per channel and role keeps the component from becoming the integration God object.
best_practices: Publish an application-facing interface (domain types, plain methods) and keep the messaging client's types out of it.
Make acknowledgements and failure policy explicit: ack only after successful handling, nack or reject with a dead-letter destination, and make handlers idempotent because redelivery is normal.
Choose the consumption style deliberately: event-driven consumption for latency, polling when you must control the rate or need externally controlled transactions.
Keep the endpoint thin: delegate payload translation to a Messaging Mapper and routing to the broker; keep business logic in the application.
Own connection and session lifecycle: reconnect with backoff, re-register consumers after recovery, and surface connection loss as a health signal instead of silently stopping.
Cover the endpoint with message-level tests - payload round-trip, malformed message, duplicate delivery, handler failure - against a broker double or an embedded broker.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Message Endpoint (Messaging Endpoints chapter).
